title: The mountain of Moriah (Genesis 22:1–19)
hook: the hardest story: Abraham is tested, a ram is caught, and the place is named the Lord will provide

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hagar in the wilderness, a bowshot away, until her eyes were opened, and your line was there's a well. Who did you ask for help? Day three hundred fifty-seven, the end of the week.

Some stories you can tell a child at bedtime. Some you can't. Genesis twenty-two is the second kind. Jews call it the Akedah, the binding. Christians, Jews and Muslims each have their own tellings of a father asked to give up his son. Painters and philosophers keep coming back to it. It is a hard text, and rereading doesn't make it softer. So today isn't about solving it. It's about reading it slowly, saying plainly what the text says and what it doesn't, and sitting with it.
screen: `NOT A BEDTIME STORY.` → `THE AKEDAH, THE BINDING.` → `NOT SOLVING IT, SITTING WITH IT.`

segments.voice: It opens, in the King James Bible: "God did tempt Abraham." Tempt here means test, and the reader is told that before Abraham knows anything. God calls, and Abraham answers, here am I. Then the command, every phrase heavier than the last: "Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest." Go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there. Early in the morning, Abraham saddles his donkey. Three days of walking. Isaac carries the wood. Abraham carries the fire and the knife. And then father and son speak. Isaac: "Behold the fire and the wood: but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham: "My son, God will provide himself a lamb." And the two of them went together, the text says, twice. At the top, Abraham builds the altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife, and the angel of the LORD calls his name twice: Abraham, Abraham. Lay not thine hand upon the lad. He looks up, and there is a ram caught in a thicket by its horns. He names the place Jehovah-jireh, in the King James Bible: the LORD will see, the LORD will provide. In Hebrew it's the same verb as Hagar's El Roi, the God who sees. Readers have answered this story in many ways. Jews read it at the new year and remember Abraham's faith and Isaac's binding. Christian tradition has heard Good Friday in it: a son carrying wood up a hill, and a lamb provided. And readers in each tradition have found it deeply troubling. The text doesn't tell us what Abraham felt, how old Isaac was, or whether Sarah knew. It doesn't answer every question. That's the end of a week of promises: stars, a seeing God, strangers, a bargain, a laugh, a well, and this mountain.
screen: `GOD DID TEMPT: GOD TESTED.` · `WHERE IS THE LAMB?` · `A RAM CAUGHT IN A THICKET.` · `YIREH: THE LORD WILL SEE.` · then, large: `GOD WILL PROVIDE HIMSELF A LAMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with a story you can't resolve. Settle, and breathe. You don't have to make sense of Moriah today. Just let it sit there, unresolved, like a stone in your hand. Then, if you want, bring another story alongside it: something in your own life, or the world's, that you can't explain or tie up. Don't argue it closed. Don't force a moral. Just keep breathing next to it, the way the father and son walked together. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
The mountain of Moriah. Where Abraham is tested, Isaac is bound and spared, a ram is caught, and the place is named the LORD will provide.
Your line: the lord will provide. Today, when a question can't be answered, let it stay a question for now, and walk on together with someone. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Many churches read Genesis 22 during Lent or at the Easter Vigil, where it is heard alongside the story of Good Friday.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about Abraham's obedience with a happy ending.
what it means: a hard story, read slowly, with its silences kept: a test, a binding, a ram, a place named the LORD will provide.
what a scholar hears: yireh, will see, the same verb as El Roi; read by Jews at the new year as the Akedah, and by Christian tradition alongside Good Friday.

notes: Sensitive story. The script deliberately does not resolve it; confirm tone and that no tradition is ranked.

'Christians, Jews and Muslims have each wrestled with their own tellings': the Qur'an (37:99–111) tells of a son, unnamed there; Muslim tradition widely identifies him as Ishmael. Script keeps it general. Confirm.
The Akedah is read on Rosh Hashanah (second day). Confirm 'Jews read it at the new year'.
'The only conversation between them in the whole Bible': Isaac and Abraham's only recorded exchange (22:7–8). Confirm.
'And the two of them went together' appears in 22:6 and 22:8. Confirm.
22:14 KJV renders the name 'Jehovahjireh'; the script gives 'Adonai yireh' as the Jewish reading of the divine name. Confirm presentation.
Week end (351–357): look-back at the end of the teach. Confirm.
